strengths: The manuscript presents a timely and practically significant systems contribution for fine-grained, sparse MoE training, combining activation-memory reduction, IO-aware GPU kernels, and tile-aware routing. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b434dbb1be3f4275a9370a2a893dd38c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reformulated backward computation is well motivated and appears mathematically sound in its central idea: computing router-score gradients through the smaller expert hidden dimension avoids caching the large per-expert down-projection outputs. Reported activation-memory savings are substantial, reaching 45% over ScatterMoE in the highlighted 7B configuration.

The kernel design demonstrates considerable technical depth, including fused gathers for variable-M and variable-K grouped GEMMs, heavy epilogue fusion, asynchronous IO, ping-pong scheduling, and an efficient aggregation strategy.

The empirical kernel evaluation is unusually broad across model scales, expert granularities, and strong baselines including ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and DeepGEMM. Runtime breakdowns and component-level ablations help attribute the speedups to specific design decisions.

The token-rounding experiments cover several model sizes, sparsity settings, routing baselines, rounding rules, microbatch sizes, and tile sizes. Training for up to 100B tokens provides meaningful evidence that the routing modification can preserve language-model quality in the studied regime.
The reported 64-H100 training throughput approaching ScatterMoE on 96 H100s indicates potentially important practical impact beyond isolated microbenchmarks.
weaknesses: The token-rounding efficiency evidence excludes router execution time even though the method requires an additional expert-wise sorting and reassignment stage. Consequently, the reported 9.4–15.9% improvements describe the MoE computation kernels rather than demonstrated end-to-end layer or training speedups. This is a major gap for one of the three headline contributions.

The default deterministic nearest-rounding rule does not generally preserve the total number of routed token-expert assignments in expectation; no distributional assumption or proof establishes the paper's claim. Model TFLOPS based on the resulting assignment count may therefore conflate removal of padding with changes in useful computation. The balanced-rounding variant partly addresses this issue but is not the default evaluated for speed.

Quality comparisons use apparently single training runs without uncertainty estimates. Many reported differences between token rounding and token choice are only a few tenths of an accuracy point, so the strong claim of no accuracy loss is not statistically established. Evaluation is also limited to models of at most 1.8B parameters despite performance claims motivated by much larger MoEs.

The specialized top-K kernel packs indices into lower FP32 mantissa bits and explicitly assumes sufficiently separated logits. This operation can change ordering for close scores, yet the paper does not report exact agreement rates against a reference top-K implementation, numerical corner cases, or resulting model-quality effects.

Hardware validation is narrower than the framing suggests. Nearly all reported results are from H100 GPUs, with no Blackwell benchmarks despite repeated claims of a Hopper-and-Blackwell design. Distributed evaluation contains only one cross-GPU-count comparison and lacks same-hardware-count end-to-end baselines, expert-parallel experiments, communication costs, and scaling curves.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the promised repository link is blank, and important benchmarking details such as timing protocol, repetitions, variance, GPU clock/power settings, and exact end-to-end baseline configurations are missing.

Several presentation inconsistencies weaken confidence in otherwise plausible results: Algorithm 3 and Equation 12 write a dimensionally invalid transpose in the dW2 expression, Figure 13's caption says gathered expert inputs are cached despite the central claim that they are not, and the 'minimum possible' activation-memory claim is stronger than the provided lower-bound argument.

strengths: The paper targets an important systems bottleneck for increasingly fine-grained and sparse MoE models, with a clear analysis connecting granularity and sparsity to arithmetic intensity, activation memory, and tile-padding waste.
The kernel design is technically substantial: fused gathers, alternative gradient computation, asynchronous I/O, ping-pong scheduling, and aggregation choices are explained in useful detail.
The evaluation includes several relevant MoE implementations and extensive kernel-level breakdowns, ablations, model configurations, and memory measurements.
The alternative computation of router-score gradients appears mathematically sound and can meaningfully reduce cached activations and memory traffic.
Token rounding is an interesting hardware-aware routing idea, and the paper evaluates it across multiple model sizes, sparsity levels, rounding rules, microbatch sizes, and tile sizes.
weaknesses: The headline end-to-end evidence is inadequate. The only full-training throughput comparison uses SonicMoE on 64 H100s versus ScatterMoE on 96 H100s, rather than a controlled comparison on identical hardware. Timing methodology, variance, utilization, and same-scale baseline results are missing, so the claimed 50% training-throughput improvement is not convincingly established.

The reported token-rounding speedups exclude routing itself, even though the method requires top-K selection followed by expert-wise sorting and rounding over the token-expert matrix. No end-to-end step-time result includes this overhead, making the claimed additional training-throughput improvement potentially misleading.

Token-rounding quality conclusions rely on single runs without uncertainty estimates. Many downstream differences are small and likely within training/evaluation variance. Evaluation is also restricted to models of at most 1.8B parameters, despite efficiency claims emphasizing much larger MoEs.

Token rounding is batch-dependent and not directly usable for autoregressive decoding; evaluation switches to ordinary token-choice routing. The resulting train-test mismatch is only empirically checked at modest scale, while implications for distributed expert parallelism, communication balance, and realistic sequence batching are not evaluated.

The paper repeatedly claims Blackwell support and discusses Blackwell-specific implementation details, but presents no Blackwell measurements. Nearly all empirical evidence is from a single GPU generation, H100.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript claims open-source kernels, but the GitHub link is blank. It also omits essential benchmarking details such as repeated-trial statistics, warmup and timing procedures, H100 variant and clock settings, and comprehensive software configurations.

The custom top-K kernel deliberately overwrites lower FP32 mantissa bits with indices and only assumes that score gaps exceed the resulting perturbation. It can therefore change assignments for near-tied scores, yet the paper provides no exactness analysis or disagreement-rate measurements against a correct top-K implementation.

The 'minimum possible activation memory' claim is stronger than justified: there is no lower-bound proof, transient Y storage is discounted under assumptions about layer count, and the accounting is internally unclear about whether gathered activations are cached. Comparisons also do not examine checkpointed or recomputation-based alternatives.

Several important claims are supported predominantly by synthetic single-layer, single-GPU configurations without expert parallelism. These results do not establish corresponding gains for the large distributed MoEs used to motivate the work.

There are technical and presentation inconsistencies, including a dimensionally invalid expression for dW2 in Algorithm 3, conflicting parameter labels for the routing experiments, and claims of 'no accuracy loss' that exceed the statistically unsupported evidence. Overall, the work contains promising engineering ideas, but its central end-to-end, routing-speed, correctness, and reproducibility claims are insufficiently validated for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely systems bottleneck for increasingly fine-grained and sparse MoE models, with clear practical significance.

SonicMoE combines several technically meaningful contributions: a mathematically equivalent, memory-efficient backward computation; fused gather and epilogue operations; asynchronous IO/computation overlap; an optimized top-K kernel; and tile-aware token-rounding routing.

The evaluation is unusually broad at the kernel level, covering forward and backward passes, activation memory, multiple model scales and expert configurations, detailed runtime breakdowns, and strong baselines including ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and optimized DeepGEMM variants.

The reported improvements are substantial: up to 45% lower per-layer activation memory for the fine-grained 7B setting, consistently higher H100 throughput, and a compelling end-to-end result where 64 H100s approach the throughput of ScatterMoE on 96 H100s.

The token-rounding method is evaluated beyond throughput: the paper studies several model sizes and sparsity regimes, trains for 20B–100B tokens, reports validation perplexity and 11 downstream tasks, and includes useful ablations over rounding rules, microbatch size, and tile size.

The exposition is technically detailed and generally clear, with algorithms, computational graphs, profiling results, configuration tables, and derivations that make the design understandable. The stated release of the kernels would further strengthen reproducibility.
weaknesses: The token-rounding speed measurements explicitly exclude router runtime, although token rounding requires an additional expert-wise sorting stage. Consequently, the reported 9.4%–15.9% improvements in MoE-kernel time do not establish comparable end-to-end training speedups; measuring the complete routing-plus-MoE path is important.

The end-to-end training evidence is limited to one 7B configuration and compares different GPU counts rather than reporting a controlled same-hardware comparison. Most conclusions otherwise rely on isolated single-layer benchmarks, so broader full-model measurements would make the systems claims more convincing.

The quality differences between token rounding and token-choice routing are often small, but results appear to come from single runs and lack uncertainty estimates. This weakens the strong claim that routing quality is preserved, particularly because performance degrades when the average tokens per expert approach one tile.

Despite discussion of both Hopper and Blackwell, the presented performance experiments are on H100 GPUs. There is no Blackwell benchmark, and portability to other GPU generations, precisions such as FP8, or non-NVIDIA accelerators is not established.

Distributed expert-parallel execution and communication overlap are not evaluated, even though these are central in large production MoE training. The FSDP experiment does not substitute for demonstrating performance under expert-parallel all-to-all communication.

The optimized top-K implementation stores indices in low FP32 mantissa bits and assumes sufficiently separated routing scores. The paper acknowledges that close scores can violate this assumption but does not quantify routing mismatches or provide an exactness analysis.

Some claims are overstated: “minimum possible” activation memory depends on excluding recomputation and amortizing a transient Y buffer, while the paper itself notes conditions under which that buffer is hidden. The presentation also contains minor inconsistencies, such as the Figure 13 caption stating that gathered inputs are cached despite the main text emphasizing their elimination.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck: efficient training of increasingly fine-grained and sparse MoE models.
Presents a strong systems co-design spanning backward-pass dataflow, fused grouped-GEMM kernels, asynchronous I/O scheduling, aggregation, top-K selection, and hardware-aware routing.
The backward formulation is mathematically explained and substantially reduces cached activations; reported memory savings are meaningful, especially for fine-grained configurations.

Kernel evaluation is unusually extensive, covering forward and backward passes, several model scales and granularities, H100 and B300 GPUs, detailed runtime breakdowns, and comparisons against ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM, Triton, and cuBLAS references.
A 64-H100 training experiment provides valuable evidence that the kernel improvements can translate beyond isolated microbenchmarks.

The token-rounding method is simple and practically motivated, and its language-model experiments span multiple sparsity settings, training budgets up to 100B tokens, several routing baselines, and useful microbatch/tile-size ablations.
The appendix provides equations, implementation comparisons, exact benchmark configurations, pinned baseline revisions, and training hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claimed end-to-end benefit of token rounding is not convincingly established because the principal throughput benchmarks explicitly exclude routing time. Token rounding requires an additional expert-wise ranking over tokens, whose cost could offset the reported 9–16% MoE-kernel gain; total training-step throughput including this router should be reported.

The novelty of individual kernel ingredients is somewhat incremental: ping-pong scheduling and gather/epilogue fusion are established techniques, while the paper acknowledges that Megatron can follow a similar score-gradient computation path. The contribution is strongest as a careful integration and optimization rather than as wholly new primitives.

The multi-GPU end-to-end evidence is limited to one 7B configuration and compares 64 SonicMoE GPUs with 96 ScatterMoE GPUs. Same-hardware-count throughput, scaling efficiency, memory usage, and statistical variability would make this result substantially more convincing.

The evaluation omits expert parallelism and communication-computation overlap, even though these are central to training the largest sparse MoEs used to motivate the work. Most results therefore demonstrate single-device MoE-layer efficiency rather than full frontier-scale training behavior.

The claim that token rounding causes no quality loss is stronger than the evidence: downstream differences are small, but no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided, and evaluation switches from token rounding during training to token-choice routing at inference.

The 'minimum possible activation memory' statement is conditional on no GEMM recomputation and on amortizing a materialized temporary Y across sufficiently many layers. These qualifications make the headline claim less general, particularly for shallow models or large K.

Benchmark fairness depends partly on author-built wrappers such as DeepGEMM++, and some baselines cannot run certain configurations. More discussion of tuning effort, workspace allocation, numerical tolerances, warmup/repetition protocol, and latency variance is needed.
All primary kernels use BF16 on NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell GPUs. The lack of FP8/MX formats and non-NVIDIA evaluation narrows the immediate applicability relative to current large-scale MoE practice.

strengths: The paper addresses an important systems bottleneck for increasingly fine-grained and sparse MoE models. The arithmetic-intensity analysis and discussion of how granularity and sparsity increase IO and tile-padding costs are clear and practically relevant.

The backward-pass reformulation is mathematically motivated and reduces activation storage by avoiding materialized gathered inputs and down-projection outputs. The reported 45% memory reduction for a fine-grained 7B configuration is meaningful.

The kernel engineering is substantial: gather fusion, fused epilogues, asynchronous IO, Hopper ping-pong scheduling, and Blackwell-specific implementation choices form a coherent design rather than an isolated optimization.

Kernel benchmarks cover H100 and B300 GPUs, several model-scale configurations, forward and backward passes, and numerous baselines. The appendix provides useful component-level ablations, including grouped GEMM, gathering, aggregation, and top-K kernels.

The token-rounding experiments include several model sizes, sparsity settings, routing baselines, and ablations over rounding rules, microbatch sizes, and tile sizes. These results suggest that routing quality can often be preserved when the average tokens per expert substantially exceeds one tile.

The manuscript is generally well organized, and the derivation of the alternative router-gradient computation is easy to follow. weaknesses: The central efficiency evidence for token rounding excludes the routing computation itself. Section 6.3.3 explicitly benchmarks the MoE main kernels “without router,” although token rounding first performs ordinary token-choice top-K and then requires an additional expert-wise ordering of tokens. Consequently, the claimed 9.4–15.9% end-to-end improvements and the headline claim of up to 16% additional training speedup are not established. Full layer and training-step timings including both routing algorithms are necessary and could materially change the conclusion.

The practical end-to-end evaluation is insufficient. The only full-training throughput comparison contrasts SonicMoE on 64 H100s with ScatterMoE on 96 H100s, rather than comparing methods on identical hardware, batch configuration, and distributed setup. Most evidence is single-layer microbenchmarking; Figure 5 additionally excludes inter-kernel stream bubbles. There is no matched end-to-end comparison on H100 or B300 and no evaluation with expert parallelism or communication, despite those being central to large-scale MoE training.

The “without quality loss” conclusion for token rounding is too strong. Quality is evaluated only up to 1.8B parameters, with no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance analysis. Many downstream differences are small and noisy, and the authors themselves observe degradation when the average expert load is one tile. The train-time expert-choice-like padding/dropping and inference-time token-choice mismatch therefore remains insufficiently validated at the scales targeted by the systems claims.

The paper does not report systematic numerical-correctness tests against a reference implementation for forward outputs and every backward gradient across shapes and routing patterns. This is especially important for heavily fused custom BF16 kernels, altered reduction orders, packed-key top-K sorting, and hardware-specific asynchronous schedules.

Several ingredients have limited standalone novelty: ping-pong scheduling and asynchronous IO overlap are established techniques, gather and activation fusion appear in earlier MoE kernels, and the efficient router-gradient algebra is acknowledged as also being used by Megatron. The integration is valuable, but the novelty claims should more carefully distinguish new algorithms from engineering adaptation and combination.

Benchmark reproducibility is incomplete. The paper provides shapes and some library versions but lacks a clear timing protocol, repetitions and variance, GPU clock/power settings, compilation settings, and matched memory-accounting methodology. The anonymized manuscript also leaves the promised repository link blank, preventing artifact verification during review.

The “minimum possible activation memory” language is stronger than justified. The comparison is tied to a particular no-recomputation execution model, treats some buffers as recyclable or transient, and reports per-layer rather than full-model peak memory. A complete end-to-end memory measurement under identical training settings would better support the practical claim.

Overall, the kernel work is promising and technically substantial, but the omitted token-rounding overhead and lack of controlled end-to-end comparisons affect central claims rather than peripheral details. These shortcomings place the submission marginally below the acceptance threshold in its present form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely systems problem: fine-grained, sparse MoEs increasingly suffer from activation-memory, I/O, and tile-padding overheads that are not captured by FLOP-based efficiency analyses.

SonicMoE combines several meaningful technical contributions: an algebraically equivalent backward computation that avoids caching large activations, fused gather/epilogue operations, Hopper- and Blackwell-specific I/O–compute overlap, and tile-aware token-rounding routing.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a kernel paper. It covers H100 and B300 GPUs, forward and backward passes, model configurations from roughly 1.4B to 120B parameters, configurations drawn from recent MoEs up to 685B parameters, and numerous strong baselines including ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM, and Triton implementations.

The improvements are practically substantial: up to 45% lower per-layer activation memory for the fine-grained 7B setting, large backward-pass gains over ScatterMoE and MoMoE, and meaningful improvements over an optimized DeepGEMM-based pipeline on both GPU generations.

The paper includes an end-to-end distributed-training result, reporting 213B tokens/day on 64 H100s, in addition to isolated kernel throughput. This materially strengthens the practical relevance of the work.

Token rounding is well motivated by tile quantization, comes with a clear per-expert deviation bound, and is supported by extensive quality experiments, comparisons with token-choice, token-dropping, and expert-choice alternatives, and ablations over rounding rules, microbatch sizes, and tile sizes.

The presentation is technically detailed and largely reproducible: algorithms, computational derivations, benchmark shapes, training hyperparameters, implementation choices, and extensive kernel-level breakdowns are provided. The stated open-source release further increases likely impact.
weaknesses: The strongest end-to-end comparison uses SonicMoE on 64 H100s versus ScatterMoE on 96 H100s. While compelling operationally, it is not a controlled same-hardware-count scaling comparison; equal-GPU throughput, scaling efficiency, and wall-clock breakdowns would make the end-to-end claim substantially stronger.

Most performance conclusions concern BF16 on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell hardware. The paper does not evaluate FP8/MX formats, other accelerator families, or broader portability, so the implementation's impact is presently tied to a narrow hardware and precision regime.

Distributed evaluation uses FSDP/ZeRO-3 and does not study expert parallelism, all-to-all communication, or communication–computation overlap. These effects can dominate large production MoEs and may change the realized benefit of the single-layer optimizations.

The token-rounding quality evidence reaches only about 1.8B parameters and consists of apparently single training runs without error bars or seed-level variability. Small differences in perplexity and average downstream accuracy therefore should not be interpreted as statistically established improvements over token-choice routing.

Token-rounding throughput plots exclude router cost, while the method adds an expert-wise sorting stage. Although router kernels are discussed separately, reporting full layer and end-to-end training speedups including the complete routing pipeline across all sparsity settings would better support the headline gains.

The claim of a minimum activation footprint is conditional on avoiding GEMM recomputation and on amortizing/recycling a transient routed-output buffer across sufficiently many MoE layers. The paper explains these assumptions, but the headline could state them more explicitly.

Token rounding can degrade quality when the expected tokens per expert approach one tile and requires switching back to token-choice routing for autoregressive inference. These limitations constrain its applicability in especially sparse or small-microbatch regimes.
